To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

jumps are more likely to occur in stocks with low liquidity, high trading volume, and low return variability and that the magnitude of jumps is positively related to trading activity and negatively related to firm size, liquidity and return variability.
small, illiquidsmall, illiquid, growth, and high-volatility stocks are more susceptible to large jumps in stock prices.
the magnitude of stock price jumps decreases with firm characteristics that are associated with low liquidity, low trading volume, low turnover, high size, and high book-to-market ratio.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
the cross-section of jump dynamics around quarterly earnings announcements.
the dynamics of stock prices and the determinants of jumps.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
jumps are a function of both the firm and market conditions.
the more liquid the stock, the less likely it is to jump, but when it jumps, the jump is larger.
small, illiquide, and growth firms are more likely to jump than large, liquid, and value firms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cross-section of jump dynamics is related to firm characteristics and that this relationship is not driven by information shocks.

small, growth, illiquid, high-turnover, and high-volume firms are more susceptible to large, negative jumps around earnings announcements, and that the magnitude of these jumps decreases with firm liquidity and return volatility.
the cross-section of jumps is driven by a combination of liquidity, trading volume, turnover, and firm size.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cross section of jump sizes can be explained by firm size, liquidity and trading activity.
jumps around earnings announcements are not a uniform phenomenon, but instead vary across firms in a systematic way that is consistent with a number of well-known stylized facts in the literature.
the cross-section of jump risk is driven by the firm characteristics that make it difficult for investors to process the information in stock prices.
